name: asr-post-processor-transformations
source: context/transcript-raw.txt (voice note dictated 2026-10-16), refined in docs/spec.md
input_assumption: Raw output of nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2 (via the Whisperian Android app): already punctuated and cased, numbers mostly normalised, no paragraph breaks.

owners.postprocessor: This model. Text in, text out, meaning preserved.
owners.asr-finetune: Fixed by fine-tuning the ASR model, because the audio is needed to decide (homophones, vocabulary, code-switched words).
owners.llm-pass: A later, optional, system-prompted LLM pass that reshapes the text for a target format or style. Not this model's job.
owners.out-of-scope: Not handled anywhere in this project, or already handled by the ASR model or a deterministic regex pass.

layers.1: Foundational. Every output gets these. Safe for a WhatsApp message and a 2,000-word report alike.
layers.2: Light editorial cleanup. Still meaning-preserving, but involves judgement about what the speaker meant to keep. Shipped as a separate model variant or flag so it can be A/B tested for going too far.
layers.3: Editing proper: restructure, restyle, reformat. Owned by the llm-pass, listed only to mark the boundary.

fields.id: Stable identifier; used as a label in training data (which transformations were applied to a pair).
fields.layer: 1, 2 or 3; null for items owned outside the post-processor.
fields.owner: One of the keys in owners.
fields.regex_coverage: none | partial | full: how much of it a deterministic pass in danielrosehill/ASR-Regex-Post-Processing can already do.
fields.status: in-scope | experimental (in scope for an A/B test, may be dropped) | excluded

transformations.description: Delete filled pauses and filler words (um, uh, erm) and filler uses of 'like' / 'you know' that carry no meaning. Regex handles the unambiguous tokens; the model handles the context-dependent ones ('like' as a verb or comparison stays).

example.raw: So, um, I was, like, thinking we could move the call to Thursday.
example.clean: So I was thinking we could move the call to Thursday.

transformations.description: Collapse immediate word or short-phrase repetition produced while speaking ('the the', 'in the. In the. In the').

example.raw: I think those should definitely be included in the. In the. In the. In the transcription.
example.clean: I think those should definitely be included in the transcription.

transformations.description: Remove an abandoned start (the reparandum) when the speaker immediately restarts the same clause. Keep only the completed version.

example.raw: The reason I think I'm. I'm underscoring this is to say that it can't be too deterministic.
example.clean: The reason I'm underscoring this is to say that it can't be too deterministic.

transformations.description: Expand informal spoken contractions to their written form: gonna -> going to, wanna -> want to, gotta -> have to / got to, kinda -> kind of, sorta -> sort of, lemme -> let me, dunno -> don't know. Standard contractions (I'm, don't, it's) are kept. Regex can do gonna/wanna; gotta and 'gonna' before a noun need context.

example.raw: I'm gonna go get some beer from the fridge.
example.clean: I'm going to go get some beer from the fridge.

transformations.description: Parakeet v2 often ends a sentence at a mid-clause pause, producing a fragment and a spurious capital ('One failure pattern. Is that the way I use it', from context/transcript-raw.txt). Within one transcript the model can see both halves, so it rejoins them. Different from L-out.cross-utterance-restart, where the halves are in separate ASR sessions.

example.raw: One failure pattern. Is that I start a sentence, stop, and continue it.
example.clean: One failure pattern is that I start a sentence, stop, and continue it.

transformations.description: Insert paragraph breaks (blank line) at topic or thought shifts in long dictation. Target style: short paragraphs, one thought each (the speaker's preference, configurable later). Text under roughly 60 words stays one paragraph. Requires long training examples (30 s+ of speech, 80+ words), because short ones never contain a boundary.

example.raw: Hi Sarah, thanks for sending the contract over. I've read through it and it looks fine apart from clause four. On a separate note, are you free next Tuesday for the site visit? I can do any time after ten.
example.clean:
Hi Sarah, thanks for sending the contract over. I've read through it and it looks fine apart from clause four.

On a separate note, are you free next Tuesday for the site visit? I can do any time after ten.

transformations.description: Remove a point the speaker restates in the same breath with no added information. Distinct from L1.stutter-repetition by span length: here it is a clause or sentence, not a word.

example.raw: Today's to-do list is I need to pick up a parcel from the post office. I need to pick up a parcel from the post office and I also need to go to the pharmacy.
example.clean: Today's to-do list: I need to pick up a parcel from the post office, and I also need to go to the pharmacy.

transformations.description: Apply an explicit spoken correction and drop the corrected material: 'Tuesday, no, sorry, Wednesday', 'I mean', 'scratch that'. 'Scratch that' at the end of a sentence is a regex candidate in ASR-Regex-Post-Processing; mid-sentence corrections need the model.

example.raw: Let's meet on Tuesday, no, sorry, Wednesday at three.
example.clean: Let's meet on Wednesday at three.

transformations.description: Delete speech plainly addressed to someone else in the room, not to the transcript (signing for a delivery, answering a family member). The literature term is addressee detection / device-directed speech detection (see docs/research.md). Experimental: deletion is the costliest error class, so precision matters more than recall. If the POC shows the model deletes real content, this moves to llm-pass.

example.raw: We need to upgrade to the latest version of the API. Sure, come in. Thanks a lot, Jim. Leave the door closed. Where was I? The old version is deprecated in March.
example.clean: We need to upgrade to the latest version of the API. The old version is deprecated in March.

transformations.description: Delete self-directed recovery phrases that are not content: 'where was I?', 'what was I saying', 'hang on'. Usually co-occurs with L2.non-directed-speech.

example.raw: The invoice is due Friday. Hang on. Where was I? Right, the invoice is due Friday and it covers both months.
example.clean: The invoice is due Friday, and it covers both months.

transformations.description: Thin out habitual hedges and discourse markers ('kind of', 'sort of', 'basically', 'I guess', sentence-initial 'So,' / 'Okay, so') when they are tics rather than meaning. High risk of flattening the speaker's voice; kept only if the A/B test says it reads better.

example.raw: So basically I kind of think we should, I guess, just ship it on Monday.
example.clean: I think we should just ship it on Monday.

transformations.description: Add headings, bullet lists or sections to long dictation.

example.raw: First the budget is approved. Second the vendor is picked. Third we schedule the install.
example.clean:
## Next steps

1. Budget approved.
2. Vendor picked.
3. Install scheduled.

transformations.description: Move material so related points sit together when the speaker jumped between topics.

example.raw: The API needs upgrading. Also I need to book flights. Back to the API, it breaks on the old SDK.
example.clean:
The API needs upgrading; it breaks on the old SDK.

I also need to book flights.

transformations.description: Make it more formal, polished, concise, or fit a format (business email, blog outline). This is what danielrosehill/Text-Transformation-Prompts-300525 does with system prompts.

example.raw: Hey, just checking if you got the thing I sent yesterday.
example.clean: Dear Mr Cohen, I am writing to confirm that you received the document I sent yesterday.

transformations.description: Wrong spelling of a homophone (their/there, write/right, Parakeet errors seen in daily use). The text model cannot hear the audio and would have to guess from context; the ASR fine-tune can learn the speaker's acoustics. The Read-Aloud-Voice-Sentences dataset already has a homophone category for this.

example.raw: I need to right the report tonight.
example.clean: I need to write the report tonight.

transformations.description: Misrecognised domain vocabulary, product names and Hebrew words in English speech (makolet -> 'Micollette'). Owned by English-Hebrew-Codeswitching-Parakeet-Finetune and the vocabulary fine-tune. A regex replacement list can patch the few most frequent errors.

example.raw: I want to go to the Micollette today.
example.clean: I want to go to the makolet today.

transformations.description: Whisperian has no pause button, so the speaker stops and restarts mid-sentence; the second recording starts with a capital letter. The post-processor only sees one recording at a time and cannot know the previous one ended mid-sentence. Ruled out in the voice note. A fix would live in the app (pass the preceding text as context), not here.

example.raw: [recording 1] I wanted to ask whether [recording 2] You could send the file by Friday.
example.clean: I wanted to ask whether you could send the file by Friday.

transformations.description: Full punctuation and truecasing restoration of unpunctuated lowercase ASR output. Parakeet v2 already emits punctuation and casing, so the model only repairs errors (L1.pause-induced-sentence-breaks). If a non-punctuating ASR is ever used upstream, a dedicated punctuation model goes in front (see docs/research.md).

example.raw: can you send me the file by friday thanks
example.clean: Can you send me the file by Friday? Thanks.

transformations.description: Spoken punctuation and layout commands ('comma', 'full stop', 'new paragraph'). Deterministic; belongs in the regex pre-pass (listed under ideas in ASR-Regex-Post-Processing).

example.raw: Thanks new paragraph see you Monday full stop
example.clean:
Thanks

See you Monday.

transformations.description: Inverse text normalisation: 'three thirty pm' -> '3:30 pm', 'jane at example dot com' -> an email address. Parakeet v2 already does most of it; residual cases are regex. Training pairs must not change numbers, so the model learns to leave them alone.

example.raw: Call me at three thirty pm.
example.clean: Call me at 3:30 pm.
